args.text:
CHICAGO, May 4, 189-

_Dear Pierrepont:_ The cashier's just handed me your expense account for the month, and I tell ya, going over it fair makes a bloke's shoulders hunch up. When I said I wanted you to get a broad education, I didn't mean I wanted to buy Cambridge. Now, the bills won't send me broke, of course, but they'll send you broke unless you're dead careful.

For the last two years I've watched your accounts get heavier every month, but I haven't seen a sign of you taking honours to justify the extra running costs; and that's bad business, mate--a fair bit like feeding a no-hoper steer its own weight in corn when it won't fatten up.

I've kept my trap shut about this till now, cos I was leaning a fair bit on your own nous to stop you making a mug of yourself, the way some of these young blokes do who've never had to work for it. But just because I've sat tight, don't go getting it into your head that the old man's loaded and can wear it, cos he won't wear it once you've left uni. The sooner you bring your spending into line with what you'll be earning, the easier the two of them will find it to live together.

The only sure way a bloke gets rich quick is to have it handed to him or to inherit it. You're not getting rich that way--not till you've shown you can hold down a pretty important job with the firm, anyway; and, of course, there's only one place a man can start from for that job with Graham & Co. Doesn't matter if he's the son of the old man or the son of the cellar boss--that place is the bottom. And the bottom in the office end of this business is a seat at the mailing-desk, with eight quid every Saturday night.

I can't hand you success on a plate. It'd do you no good, and it'd do the firm harm. There's plenty of room at the top here, but there's no lift in the building. Starting off, like you are, with a beaut education, you ought to climb quicker than the bloke who hasn't got one; but there'll come a time, when you start at the factory, when you won't be able to lick stamps as fast as the other young fellas at the desk. And yet the man who hasn't licked stamps isn't fit to write letters. Naturally, that's when knowing whether the pie comes before the ice-cream, and how to drive a motor car, won't be a scrap of real use to you.

I only bring all this up cos I reckon your ideas about the terms you're coming into the firm on have puffed up a bit back East. I can give you a start, but after that you'll have to blast your own way to the front. It's all up to the man. Give some blokes a talent wrapped in a napkin to start out in business with, and they'll swap the talent for a gold brick and lose the napkin; and then there's others you could start off with just a napkin, and they'd set up in the drapery business in a small way with it, and then sweet-talk the other bloke's talent into it.

I'm proud enough to believe you've got the right sort of stuff in you, but I want to see some of it come out. You'll never make a good merchant of yourself by flipping the order the Lord laid down for us--learning the spending end of business before the earning end. Payday's always a month off for the spendthrift, and he never gets more than sixty cents out of any quid that comes his way. But to a good businessman a quid's worth one hundred and six cents, and he never spends the quid. It's the man who keeps his savings up and his expenses down who ends up buying a share in the business. That's where you'll find you're weak, if your expense accounts don't lie; and they generally don't lie in that particular way, though Baron Munchausen was the first commercial traveller, and my commercial travellers' bills still show his influence.
